subChunks.title: Context API: Sharing State Without Prop Drilling
subChunks.hookHtml: You've lifted state up, passed callbacks down, and composed components carefully. But some data — the authenticated user, the current theme, the active language — is needed everywhere. Threading it through every component becomes unworkable. Context is React's built-in solution for sharing values across the component tree without passing them as props at every level.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Creating and providing context

import { createContext, useContext, useState } from 'react';

// 1. Create the context with a default value:
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');

// 2. Provide it from a parent — all descendants can access it:
function App() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
      <PageLayout />
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

// 3. Consume it in any descendant — no props needed:
function ThemeToggle() {
  const { theme, setTheme } = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setTheme(t => t === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light')}>
      Current: {theme}
    </button>
  );
}

Custom context hook — the standard pattern

Wrapping useContext in a custom hook gives better error messages and a cleaner import API:

// In ThemeContext.jsx:
export const ThemeContext = createContext(null);

export function ThemeProvider({ children }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
      {children}
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useTheme() {
  const context = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (!context) {
    throw new Error('useTheme must be used within a ThemeProvider');
  }
  return context;
}

// In any component — clean and safe:
const { theme, setTheme } = useTheme();

When to use Context — and when not to

Vex: "Context is not a state management system. It's a dependency injection system. It solves prop drilling — not complex state orchestration. The most common Context misuse I see: using it for state that changes frequently (like a list of items a user is editing). Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes. For high-frequency state, use a dedicated state manager or keep state local."

Good uses for Context:

  • Authentication state (current user, isLoggedIn)
  • Theme (dark/light mode)
  • Language / locale
  • Feature flags
  • App-wide configuration that rarely changes

Poor uses for Context:

  • A list that items are added to / removed from frequently
  • Form state
  • Frequently updated counters or real-time data

Performance: splitting contexts

If your context value changes frequently, split it. Consumers of the stable parts won't re-render when only the dynamic part changes:

// ❌ One context — AuthStateContext changes on every request,
//    causing every useAuth() consumer to re-render:
<AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, loading, refetch }}>

// ✅ Two contexts — most components only need the stable user:
<AuthUserContext.Provider value={user}>
  <AuthActionsContext.Provider value={{ loading, refetch }}>
    {children}
  </AuthActionsContext.Provider>
</AuthUserContext.Provider>

storyBeats.text: Grand Archmage Solomon appears at Vex's workshop for the first time. He holds up a tangled web of scroll-ropes — props passed through a dozen components.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: The authenticated wizard's identity. The academy's chosen theme. The active tongue. These values do not belong to one component — they belong to the entire system. Passing them through every doorway is not architecture. It is chaos.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Context solves prop drilling for values that many components need. Create the context, provide it near the root, consume it anywhere below with useContext. No intermediate props. But use it with discipline — every consumer re-renders when the context value changes. Wrap it in a custom hook, and be precise about what you put in it.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain React Context to a colleague who only knows prop drilling. What problem does it solve? Walk through the three steps (create, provide, consume). Then explain the main performance caveat and how splitting contexts addresses it.

questions.prompt: When a Context value changes, which components re-render?
options: All components that call useContext() with that specific context
All components in the entire application
Only the Provider component and its direct children
Only components that are currently visible on screen
questions.answer: All components that call useContext() with that specific context
questions.explanation: React re-renders every component that subscribed to a context (via useContext) when that context's value changes. Components in between that don't call useContext are not re-rendered. This is why putting frequently-changing state in context can cause performance problems — many consumers may re-render unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: What does `createContext(null)` return and what is the `null` argument?
options: A Context object; null is the default value used when a component consumes the context without a Provider above it
A Context object; null disables the context so it can only be used when a Provider is present
A Provider component; null sets the initial state to empty
A hook factory; null means the context will not trigger re-renders
questions.answer: A Context object; null is the default value used when a component consumes the context without a Provider above it
questions.explanation: The argument to createContext is the default value — returned by useContext when there is no matching Provider above the consumer in the tree. null is a common choice for contexts that require a Provider (your custom hook can then throw a helpful error). A meaningful default (like 'light' for a theme) lets components work without a Provider in tests or Storybook.

questions.prompt: Why do most production codebases wrap `useContext` in a custom hook instead of calling it directly?
options: To throw a clear error when the hook is used outside its Provider, and to give consumers a cleaner import API
Because useContext cannot be called directly — it requires a wrapper
To improve performance by memoizing the context value automatically
To avoid importing the Context object in every consumer file
questions.answer: To throw a clear error when the hook is used outside its Provider, and to give consumers a cleaner import API
questions.explanation: Without the wrapper, using useContext outside a Provider silently returns the default value (often null), causing confusing null reference errors. The wrapper throws a descriptive error immediately. As a bonus, consumers import useTheme() rather than both useContext and ThemeContext — one import, not two.

questions.prompt: An AuthContext provides `{ user, isLoading, refetch }`. Many components only need `user`, but `isLoading` changes on every request. What is the performance implication and the fix?
options: All useContext(AuthContext) consumers re-render on every request. Fix: split into UserContext (stable) and AuthStatusContext (dynamic) — most components only subscribe to UserContext
There is no issue — React only re-renders components that use the changed value
Memoize the context value with useMemo to prevent unnecessary re-renders
Move refetch outside the context to prevent isLoading changes from propagating
questions.answer: All useContext(AuthContext) consumers re-render on every request. Fix: split into UserContext (stable) and AuthStatusContext (dynamic) — most components only subscribe to UserContext
questions.explanation: Context doesn't do value-level change detection — any change to the Provider's value prop triggers a re-render in all consumers. Since isLoading toggles true/false on every request, every useContext(AuthContext) component re-renders twice per request. Splitting contexts means components needing only the user object (stable across requests) subscribe to UserContext and are never re-rendered by loading state changes.

subChunks.title: Performance: memo, useMemo, and useCallback
subChunks.hookHtml: React is fast by default. Most apps never need manual optimisation. But when a component renders too often, or an expensive calculation runs on every keystroke, you need to know when and how to intervene — without making the code harder to read than the problem it solves.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
How React decides to re-render

A component re-renders when:

  • Its own state changes
  • Its parent re-renders (even if props didn't change — by default)
  • A context it subscribes to changes

This default behaviour is correct and efficient for most components. The tools below are for the cases where it isn't.

React.memo — skip re-renders when props haven't changed

import { memo } from 'react';

// Without memo: re-renders every time the parent re-renders
function ExpensiveList({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map(i => <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}

// With memo: only re-renders if items actually changed (by reference)
const ExpensiveList = memo(function ExpensiveList({ items }) {
  return <ul>{items.map(i => <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>)}</ul>;
});

memo does a shallow comparison of props. If all props are the same reference as before, the re-render is skipped. This means memo only helps when the parent is re-rendering but the memoised component's props genuinely haven't changed.

useMemo — cache expensive calculations

import { useMemo } from 'react';

function QuestAnalytics({ quests }) {
  // ❌ Recalculates on every render — even unrelated state changes
  const stats = computeHeavyStats(quests);

  // ✅ Only recalculates when quests changes
  const stats = useMemo(() => computeHeavyStats(quests), [quests]);

  return <div>{stats.averageXP} avg XP</div>;
}

useMemo caches a value and only recomputes it when the listed dependencies change. Use it when a calculation is genuinely expensive (takes measurable time) — not for simple filters or array operations.

useCallback — stable function references

import { useCallback } from 'react';

function ParentList({ items }) {
  // ❌ New function reference on every render — memo'd children always re-render
  const handleDelete = (id) => setItems(prev => prev.filter(i => i.id !== id));

  // ✅ Stable reference — memo'd children can skip re-renders
  const handleDelete = useCallback(
    (id) => setItems(prev => prev.filter(i => i.id !== id)),
    [] // No dependencies — functional update reads latest state
  );

  return items.map(item => (
    <MemoizedItem key={item.id} item={item} onDelete={handleDelete} />
  ));
}

useCallback caches a function reference. It is most useful when passing callbacks to memoized child components — without it, a new function reference on every parent render defeats memo.

The golden rule — measure before optimising

Vex: "I will tell you the same thing every experienced React developer wishes someone had told them earlier: do not add memo, useMemo, or useCallback until you have measured a real performance problem with the React DevTools Profiler. These tools add overhead. Wrapping every component and function 'just in case' makes the code harder to read and can actually slow things down. Profile first. Optimise precisely."

Quick reference: which tool for which problem

// Component re-renders even when props haven't changed:
const MyComp = memo(MyComp);

// Expensive calculation runs on every render:
const result = useMemo(() => expensiveCalc(data), [data]);

// Function reference changes every render, defeating memo on children:
const fn = useCallback(() => doThing(dep), [dep]);

storyBeats.text: The profiler shows a component tree where a small counter update causes half the app to re-render. Vex points at the flame chart.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: React is fast by default — most apps never need these tools. But when you do need them, you need to use the right one. memo skips a component's re-render when its props haven't changed. useMemo caches an expensive calculation. useCallback stabilises a function reference so memo'd children don't re-render unnecessarily.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The mandatory first step is always the React DevTools Profiler. Measure what is actually slow. Then apply the precise fix. Adding memo and useCallback everywhere 'just in case' is cargo-cult optimisation — it adds overhead and makes the codebase harder to understand without necessarily solving anything.

storyBeats.speaker: When to use each

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Optimise a slow component tree:

  • A <Counter /> component has a button that increments a count. Every click re-renders the parent, which re-renders an <ExpensiveList items /> component — even though items never changes.
  • Wrap ExpensiveList in memo to stop it re-rendering when items prop hasn't changed.
  • The parent also passes an onItemClick callback down to the list. Stabilise it with useCallback so memo can do its job.
  • Add a useMemo to cache a totalXP calculation (sum of all item XP values) so it doesn't recompute on every count increment.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <SearchableList items /> component from scratch that demonstrates all three optimisation tools: memo on a ListItem child component, useMemo for the filtered results calculation, and useCallback for the item click handler passed to each ListItem. Each item has id, name, and xp. A text input filters the list by name. No scaffold.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the relationship between React.memo and useCallback. Why does memo alone not solve the problem when a parent passes a callback prop? What is the root cause, and what does useCallback fix?

questions.prompt: What does React.memo do?
options: It wraps a component and skips re-rendering if all props are shallowly equal to the previous render's props
It caches the component's rendered output and never updates it
It prevents the component's state from resetting between renders
It lazily imports the component to improve initial load time
questions.answer: It wraps a component and skips re-rendering if all props are shallowly equal to the previous render's props
questions.explanation: memo does a shallow comparison of the previous and next props. If all props are reference-equal (primitives have the same value, objects/functions are the same reference), the component's render is skipped and React reuses the previous output. It does not affect re-renders triggered by the component's own state changes.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `useMemo` and `useCallback`?
options: useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function reference
useMemo is for async operations; useCallback is for synchronous operations
useMemo is used in class components; useCallback is for function components
They are identical — useCallback(fn, deps) is shorthand for useMemo(() => fn, deps)
questions.answer: useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function reference
questions.explanation: useMemo(() => computeValue(data), [data]) caches and returns a value. useCallback((id) => doThing(id), []) caches and returns a function. Technically useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps), but they communicate different intent — value vs function — so both exist for readability.

questions.prompt: A component is wrapped in memo but still re-renders every time its parent re-renders. The only prop it receives is a callback function `onSave`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The parent creates a new function reference for onSave on every render — memo sees a new reference and re-renders
memo does not work for components that receive function props
The component's own state is changing, which bypasses memo
memo requires all props to be primitives — object and function props always trigger re-renders
questions.answer: The parent creates a new function reference for onSave on every render — memo sees a new reference and re-renders
questions.explanation: Functions in JavaScript are objects. A new arrow function `() => handleSave(id)` defined in the parent's render body creates a new reference on every render. memo's shallow comparison sees a different reference and considers the prop changed. Fix: wrap onSave in useCallback in the parent so the reference is stable between renders.

questions.prompt: When is it NOT appropriate to add useMemo to a calculation?
options: When the calculation is a simple array filter or map — the memoization overhead likely exceeds the savings
When the calculation depends on multiple state variables
When the calculation result is used in JSX directly
When the component re-renders frequently
questions.answer: When the calculation is a simple array filter or map — the memoization overhead likely exceeds the savings
questions.explanation: useMemo itself has a cost: it stores the previous result and compares dependencies on every render. For a simple filter of 10-100 items, this overhead is comparable to or greater than the calculation itself. useMemo is justified when the computation is provably expensive (measured via profiler) — sorting thousands of items, running statistical calculations, building a complex derived data structure.

subChunks.title: TypeScript with React
subChunks.hookHtml: TypeScript turns runtime errors into compile-time errors. In React, that means wrong props, missing handlers, and incorrect event types are caught before the code ever runs — not after a user finds a bug in production. Adding TypeScript to React is straightforward once you know the five patterns that cover 90% of what you'll write.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Typing component props

// Define a type or interface for props:
type ProfileCardProps = {
  name: string;
  xp: number;
  role?: string;        // Optional prop — may be undefined
  onLevelUp: () => void; // Function with no return value
};

function ProfileCard({ name, xp, role = 'Novice', onLevelUp }: ProfileCardProps) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>{role} — {xp} XP</p>
      <button onClick={onLevelUp}>Level Up</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Typing useState

// TypeScript infers the type from the initial value — no annotation needed:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);          // number
const [name, setName] = useState('');            // string
const [active, setActive] = useState(false);     // boolean

// When the initial value is null or ambiguous, annotate explicitly:
const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);

// Arrays — always annotate:
const [items, setItems] = useState<Quest[]>([]);

Typing event handlers

// React provides typed event types — always use these:
function handleClick(e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) {
  console.log(e.currentTarget.textContent);
}

function handleChange(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {
  setValue(e.target.value);
}

function handleSubmit(e: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
  e.preventDefault();
}

// Shorthand for simple handlers — TypeScript infers inline:
<input onChange={(e) => setValue(e.target.value)} />
// e is inferred as React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> automatically

Typing children

// React.ReactNode is the most permissive children type:
type LayoutProps = {
  children: React.ReactNode;
};

// React.FC is an older pattern — avoid it:
// const Layout: React.FC<LayoutProps> = ({ children }) => { ... }
// Prefer the explicit prop type instead — it's more flexible

Generic components

// A list component that works with any item type:
type ListProps<T> = {
  items: T[];
  renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode;
  keyExtractor: (item: T) => string;
};

function List<T>({ items, renderItem, keyExtractor }: ListProps<T>) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map(item => (
        <li key={keyExtractor(item)}>{renderItem(item)}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// Usage — TypeScript infers T from the items array:
<List
  items={quests}
  renderItem={(q) => <span>{q.title}</span>}
  keyExtractor={(q) => q.id.toString()}
/>

Vex: "The most common TypeScript mistake in React codebases: annotating things that TypeScript already infers. Don't write const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0) — TypeScript already knows it's a number. Save annotations for the ambiguous cases: union types, nullable values, empty arrays, and function signatures."

storyBeats.text: A quest component throws a runtime error: 'Cannot read property name of undefined.' Vex pulls up the TypeScript configuration.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: That error would have been a compile error in TypeScript — caught before a single user saw it. TypeScript with React is not about writing more code. It's about moving errors from runtime to compile time. The five patterns you need: typed props, typed useState for nullable values, typed event handlers, typed children, and generic components.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Don't over-annotate. TypeScript infers types from initial values and inline JSX. Annotate where the type is ambiguous — null initial state, empty arrays, function prop signatures. Everything else: let the compiler do the work.

storyBeats.speaker: Props type + typed event handler

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a fully TypeScript-typed <DataTable<T>> generic component from scratch. It accepts: data: T[], columns: Array<{ key: keyof T; header: string }>, and onRowClick?: (row: T) => void. It renders a <table> with headers from columns and one row per data item. No scaffold — demonstrate generic component types, optional props, and keyof T usage.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the five TypeScript patterns every React developer must know: typing props, typing useState, typing event handlers, typing children, and generic components. For each, give a one-sentence rule for when you need an explicit annotation vs when TypeScript can infer it.

questions.prompt: What TypeScript type should you use for a useState variable that starts as null but will hold a User object after fetching?
options: useState<User | null>(null)
useState<User>(null)
useState<any>(null)
useState<User>(undefined)
questions.answer: useState<User | null>(null)
questions.explanation: The initial value is null, but the type will eventually be User. TypeScript cannot infer User from null alone — it would infer null as the only possible value. The union type User | null tells TypeScript the variable can be either, requiring null checks before accessing User properties.

questions.prompt: What is the correct TypeScript type for an onChange handler on a text input?
options: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>
React.InputEvent<HTMLInputElement>
React.SyntheticEvent<HTMLInputElement>
Event<HTMLInputElement>
questions.answer: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>
questions.explanation: React provides typed event interfaces for each event type. ChangeEvent is for change events (onChange), MouseEvent is for clicks, FormEvent is for form submissions. The generic parameter specifies the element type — HTMLInputElement for text inputs, HTMLSelectElement for selects. TypeScript infers these automatically for inline handlers, but explicit types are needed for named handler functions.

questions.prompt: You define `const [items, setItems] = useState([])`. What is TypeScript's inferred type for items, and what is the problem?
options: never[] — TypeScript infers an empty array with no element type, making it impossible to push typed items
any[] — TypeScript infers any for empty arrays
undefined[] — TypeScript uses undefined for empty initial values
There is no problem — TypeScript infers the type when items are first added
questions.answer: never[] — TypeScript infers an empty array with no element type, making it impossible to push typed items
questions.explanation: TypeScript infers [] as never[] — an array that can only ever be empty. Any attempt to add items of a real type will fail type checking. Fix: provide an explicit type parameter: useState<Quest[]>([]). This tells TypeScript what type the array will contain.

questions.prompt: When is it appropriate to use `React.FC<Props>` vs an explicit prop type with a typed function signature?
options: Prefer an explicit prop type (`function Comp({ name }: Props)`) — React.FC adds implicit children, restricts the function signature, and is generally discouraged in modern React
React.FC is always preferable — it automatically types children and return value
Use React.FC for class components and explicit prop types for function components
They are identical — the choice is purely stylistic
questions.answer: Prefer an explicit prop type (`function Comp({ name }: Props)`) — React.FC adds implicit children, restricts the function signature, and is generally discouraged in modern React
questions.explanation: React.FC was common in React 17 and earlier. In modern React, it's discouraged because: (1) it used to implicitly add children to every component's props (removed in React 18's types, but still confusing), (2) it prevents using generics like function Comp<T>(), and (3) the explicit approach is more readable and flexible. The official React TypeScript docs now recommend explicit prop types.

subChunks.title: Testing with React Testing Library
subChunks.hookHtml: Tests that pass when the code works and fail when it breaks — that's the entire goal. React Testing Library is built on a single principle: test what the user sees and does, not implementation details. Learn this philosophy and the testing patterns that follow from it.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The guiding principle

React Testing Library (RTL) is deliberately opinionated: you should interact with components the way a user would — by finding elements through accessible roles, labels, and text, not by implementation details like component names or state variables.

// ❌ Testing implementation details (fragile):
expect(component.state.count).toBe(1);
expect(wrapper.find('Counter').prop('value')).toBe(1);

// ✅ Testing what the user sees (robust):
expect(screen.getByText('Count: 1')).toBeInTheDocument();

Setup and basic render

import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import Counter from './Counter';

test('shows initial count of 0', () => {
  render(<Counter />);
  expect(screen.getByText('0')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Queries — finding elements

RTL provides three query families, each with three variants:

// getBy* — throws if not found (use when element must be present)
screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add item' });
screen.getByLabelText('Email address');
screen.getByText('Submit');
screen.getByTestId('loading-spinner');

// queryBy* — returns null if not found (use to assert absence)
expect(screen.queryByText('Error')).not.toBeInTheDocument();

// findBy* — async, returns a Promise (use when element appears later)
const user = await screen.findByText('Welcome, Alice');

The query priority order (most to least preferred):

  1. getByRole — mirrors how screen readers see the page. Best for buttons, inputs, headings.
  2. getByLabelText — for form inputs associated with a label.
  3. getByText — for non-interactive text.
  4. getByTestId — last resort. Use data-testid only when no accessible query applies.

User interactions with userEvent

import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';

test('clicking + increments the counter', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<Counter />);

  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: '+' }));

  expect(screen.getByText('1')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

test('typing into the input updates displayed value', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<SearchInput />);

  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox'), 'react hooks');

  expect(screen.getByDisplayValue('react hooks')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Testing async behaviour

// Mock fetch at the module level:
global.fetch = vi.fn();

test('shows user name after successful fetch', async () => {
  fetch.mockResolvedValueOnce({
    ok: true,
    json: async () => ({ name: 'Archmage Eldrin' }),
  });

  render(<UserProfile userId={1} />);

  expect(screen.getByText('Loading...')).toBeInTheDocument();
  expect(await screen.findByText('Archmage Eldrin')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Vex: "A test that checks internal state tells you nothing about whether the user's experience is correct — the implementation could be completely rewritten and the test would break even if the UI still works perfectly. A test that checks what appears on screen tells you exactly what the user experiences. Write those tests."

storyBeats.text: A production incident notice arrives: a button that should open a modal was broken for three days before anyone noticed. No tests caught it.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: That button had no test. The state variable that tracked open/closed — that was tested. React Testing Library's philosophy: test what the user experiences, not how the component implements it. Find elements by role, label, or text. Interact by click and type. Assert on visible output.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The query priority: getByRole first — it mirrors accessibility. getByLabelText for inputs. getByText for content. getByTestId only as a last resort. A test that can only pass by reaching into implementation details is a test that will fail when you refactor correctly.

storyBeats.speaker: Test structure: render → query → interact → assert

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write three tests for a <TaskForm> component:

  • Test 1: the form renders an input and a submit button
  • Test 2: submitting the form with text calls the onAdd prop callback with the trimmed text, then clears the input
  • Test 3: submitting an empty input does not call onAdd

Use getByRole for the input and button, userEvent.type and userEvent.click for interactions, and vi.fn() for the callback mock.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a full test suite for a <PostViewer postId /> component (from RX-B2). Tests must cover: (1) loading state renders while fetching, (2) post title and body render after a successful mock fetch, (3) error message renders when the fetch fails. Mock fetch using vi.fn() with mockResolvedValueOnce / mockRejectedValueOnce. Use findBy* queries for async assertions. No scaffold.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain React Testing Library's guiding philosophy. Why does it discourage querying by component name or internal state? What is the query priority order and why does getByRole come first? Give an example of a test that tests implementation details vs one that tests user behaviour.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `getByRole`, `queryByRole`, and `findByRole`?
options: getBy throws if not found; queryBy returns null; findBy is async and waits for the element to appear
getBy is for static content; queryBy is for dynamic content; findBy is for form elements
They are identical — the prefix only affects error message formatting
findBy is deprecated in favour of getBy with async/await
questions.answer: getBy throws if not found; queryBy returns null; findBy is async and waits for the element to appear
questions.explanation: getBy* is the default for present elements — it throws a helpful error if not found, failing the test immediately. queryBy* returns null instead of throwing — use it to assert something is NOT in the document. findBy* returns a Promise and retries until the element appears or a timeout is reached — use it for elements that appear after async operations like fetches or timers.

questions.prompt: Why is `getByRole` the highest priority query in React Testing Library's recommendations?
options: Querying by role mirrors how screen readers and assistive technology navigate the page — tests that use it verify accessibility automatically
getByRole is faster than other queries because it uses native browser APIs
It is the only query that works for all HTML elements
Role-based queries are immune to CSS class and ID changes
questions.answer: Querying by role mirrors how screen readers and assistive technology navigate the page — tests that use it verify accessibility automatically
questions.explanation: Screen readers navigate by ARIA roles — button, heading, textbox, link, checkbox. A test that finds elements by role will fail if the role is wrong (e.g., a div styled as a button but not actually a button element) — catching accessibility bugs for free. It also makes tests more resilient to markup changes that don't affect user experience.

questions.prompt: A component fetches data and shows a loading state, then the data. Which query correctly waits for the data to appear?
options: await screen.findByText('Archmage Eldrin')
screen.getByText('Archmage Eldrin')
await waitFor(() => screen.getByText('Archmage Eldrin'))
Both A and C are correct
questions.answer: Both A and C are correct
questions.explanation: findByText is sugar for waitFor(() => getByText(...)). Both poll the DOM until the text appears or the timeout expires. findBy is more concise for the common case of waiting for a single element. waitFor is more flexible when you need to wait for multiple conditions or run custom assertions. Both are correct here.

questions.prompt: When is it appropriate to use `data-testid` attributes and `getByTestId` in your tests?
options: As a last resort when no accessible query (role, label, text, placeholder) can uniquely identify the element
Always — data-testid is the most stable way to query elements and should be used by default
For any element that doesn't have visible text content
Only for elements inside lists — getByRole doesn't work inside map()
questions.answer: As a last resort when no accessible query (role, label, text, placeholder) can uniquely identify the element
questions.explanation: data-testid bypasses accessibility checks — you can query any element regardless of its role or visibility. It's appropriate for custom loading spinners, containers, or elements with purely visual purpose. But defaulting to it skips the accessibility validation that role/label queries provide. Try role, then label, then text, then placeholder, then testId.

subChunks.title: State Management: Zustand
subChunks.hookHtml: Context + useReducer can handle app-wide state, but they require boilerplate and have performance limitations. Zustand is a minimal, ergonomic state management library — a global store you read from anywhere, write to from anywhere, with React re-renders scoped precisely to the data that changed. It's become the pragmatic choice for production React apps that outgrow local state.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Creating a store

import { create } from 'zustand';

const useQuestStore = create((set) => ({
  // State:
  quests: [],
  activeQuestId: null,

  // Actions:
  addQuest: (quest) => set((state) => ({
    quests: [...state.quests, quest],
  })),

  completeQuest: (id) => set((state) => ({
    quests: state.quests.map(q =>
      q.id === id ? { ...q, completed: true } : q
    ),
  })),

  setActiveQuest: (id) => set({ activeQuestId: id }),
}));

create takes a function that receives set (update state) and returns the initial state and actions as one object.

Reading from the store

// Select only what you need — component only re-renders if that slice changes:
function QuestCount() {
  const questCount = useQuestStore((state) => state.quests.length);
  return <p>{questCount} quests</p>;
}

// Read multiple values at once:
function QuestPanel() {
  const { quests, addQuest } = useQuestStore((state) => ({
    quests: state.quests,
    addQuest: state.addQuest,
  }));
}

The selector function controls which state changes trigger a re-render. A component that only selects quests.length won't re-render when activeQuestId changes.

Zustand vs Context for global state

// Context: all consumers re-render when any part of the context changes.
// Fine for rarely-changing data (theme, user).

// Zustand: components subscribe to slices — only re-render for their slice.
// Better for state that changes frequently or has many consumers.

Persisting state with zustand/middleware

import { create } from 'zustand';
import { persist } from 'zustand/middleware';

const useSettingsStore = create(
  persist(
    (set) => ({
      theme: 'light',
      setTheme: (theme) => set({ theme }),
    }),
    { name: 'settings-storage' } // localStorage key
  )
);

When to reach for Zustand

Vex: "The honest progression: start with useState (local). When siblings need to share, lift to parent. When the chain gets long, try component composition. When you need truly global state that many components read from — authentication, shopping cart, notification queue — Zustand. It's not about scale, it's about the right tool for the shape of the problem."

storyBeats.text: The academy's quest board needs to be visible from the header, the sidebar, and three different page components. Prop drilling is twelve levels deep. Vex opens a new file.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Context solves prop drilling, but every consumer re-renders when any part of the context changes. Zustand solves both problems: global state accessible from anywhere, with re-renders scoped to exactly the slice of state each component subscribed to. The store is outside React's tree. Any component can read from or write to it.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Create a store with create(). Define state and actions together. Subscribe in components with a selector that picks only what you need. The component re-renders only when its selected slice changes — nothing else.

storyBeats.speaker: Zustand store — define and consume

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Compare Zustand with React Context for global state management. When would you choose each? Explain what Zustand's selector pattern does for performance that Context cannot do natively.

questions.prompt: In Zustand, a component uses the selector `state => state.items.length`. When will it re-render?
options: Only when the items array length changes — not when item details change
Whenever any part of the store changes
Only when the component explicitly calls a store action
On every parent re-render, like normal props
questions.answer: Only when the items array length changes — not when item details change
questions.explanation: Zustand runs the selector after every store update and compares the result with the previous result. If the result is the same (items.length hasn't changed), the component doesn't re-render. A component that only selects the count won't re-render when an item's name or price changes — only when items are added or removed.

questions.prompt: In a Zustand action, why use `set(state => ({ ... }))` (function form) rather than `set({ ... })` (object form)?
options: The function form guarantees you're reading the latest state — the object form can be stale if multiple updates are queued
The object form overwrites the entire store; the function form only updates specified keys
The function form supports async actions; the object form does not
They are identical — the function form is just more verbose
questions.answer: The function form guarantees you're reading the latest state — the object form can be stale if multiple updates are queued
questions.explanation: set({ quests: [...state.quests, newQuest] }) captures state from the outer closure, which might be stale if multiple actions are dispatched before React processes them. set(prev => ({ quests: [...prev.quests, newQuest] })) receives the latest committed state from Zustand's update queue. For most actions this doesn't matter, but it's a good habit — especially for actions that depend on previous state.

questions.prompt: What does Zustand's `persist` middleware do?
options: Automatically serialises the store to localStorage (or another storage) and rehydrates it on page load
Prevents the store from being garbage collected when no components are subscribed
Persists actions to a Redux DevTools log for debugging
Caches the store's computed selectors between renders
questions.answer: Automatically serialises the store to localStorage (or another storage) and rehydrates it on page load
questions.explanation: persist wraps your store and, on every state update, serialises it to the specified storage (localStorage by default). On app load, if stored data exists under the store's name key, it rehydrates the store with that data. This gives you persistent state (cart contents, user preferences, cached data) with a single middleware addition.

questions.prompt: You need to share the authenticated user object across 30+ components. Zustand or Context — which is more appropriate, and why?
options: Either works well here — the user object rarely changes (only on login/logout), so Context's 'all consumers re-render' behaviour has minimal impact
Zustand — it always outperforms Context for any shared state
Context — Zustand is only appropriate for local component state
Neither — use a global variable and trigger re-renders manually
questions.answer: Either works well here — the user object rarely changes (only on login/logout), so Context's 'all consumers re-render' behaviour has minimal impact
questions.explanation: Context's performance limitation (all consumers re-render on every change) only matters when the shared state changes frequently. The authenticated user changes once on login and once on logout. With 30 components re-rendering twice per session, Context is perfectly fine. Zustand is a better choice when the state changes frequently (a cart, notification queue, or real-time data) and many components are subscribed.

subChunks.title: Production Patterns: Error Boundaries, Suspense, and Accessibility
subChunks.hookHtml: The difference between a demo and a production app is resilience and inclusivity. Error boundaries contain failures so one broken component doesn't crash the whole page. Suspense makes async loading states declarative. Accessibility ensures your app works for every user, not just those without disabilities. These are the patterns that separate professional work from playground code.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Error Boundaries

When a component throws an error during rendering, React unmounts the entire tree by default. Error boundaries are class components that catch errors from their children and show a fallback UI instead:

import { Component } from 'react';

class ErrorBoundary extends Component {
  state = { hasError: false, error: null };

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) {
    return { hasError: true, error };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error, info) {
    // Log to error reporting service (Sentry, Datadog, etc.):
    console.error('Boundary caught:', error, info.componentStack);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return (
        <div role="alert">
          <h2>Something went wrong.</h2>
          <button onClick={() => this.setState({ hasError: false })}>
            Try again
          </button>
        </div>
      );
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

// Usage — only errors inside are contained:
<ErrorBoundary>
  <UserDashboard />
</ErrorBoundary>

Vex: "Place error boundaries strategically, not everywhere. A boundary around each major page section prevents one broken widget from taking down the entire page. A boundary around every small component adds noise and hides bugs during development. The goal is resilience at meaningful granularity."

Suspense for async loading

import { Suspense, lazy } from 'react';

// Code splitting — load the component only when needed:
const QuestDetailPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/QuestDetailPage'));

function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading page...</div>}>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />
      </Routes>
    </Suspense>
  );
}

React.lazy + Suspense is the built-in code-splitting pattern. Large page components are loaded on demand — reducing initial bundle size.

Accessibility in React — the non-negotiables

Semantic HTML:

// ❌ Generic div with click handler — not keyboard accessible, not screen-reader announced:
<div onClick={handleSave}>Save</div>

// ✅ Semantic button — keyboard focusable, announces as button, activates on Enter/Space:
<button onClick={handleSave}>Save</button>

ARIA labels for icon-only buttons:

<button aria-label="Close modal">✕</button>
<button aria-label="Delete quest"><TrashIcon /></button>

Focus management for modals:

import { useRef, useEffect } from 'react';

function Modal({ open, onClose, children }) {
  const firstFocusRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) firstFocusRef.current?.focus();
  }, [open]);

  if (!open) return null;
  return (
    <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true">
      <button ref={firstFocusRef} onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

Accessible form fields:

// Explicit label association — required for screen readers:
<label htmlFor="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email" aria-describedby="email-hint" />
<p id="email-hint">We'll never share your email.</p>

// Error state:
<input
  aria-invalid={!!error}
  aria-describedby={error ? 'email-error' : undefined}
/>
{error && <p id="email-error" role="alert">{error}</p>}

storyBeats.text: Grand Archmage Solomon appears one final time. He doesn't look at the code — he looks at the Lighthouse accessibility report and the error monitoring dashboard.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: A component that throws crashes the page. A page that crashes loses the user. An error boundary is a promise: whatever breaks inside me will not destroy what is outside me. Place them at meaningful boundaries — major page sections, dynamic widgets, anything that fetches data.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Accessibility is not an optional enhancement. An app that only works with a mouse excludes every keyboard user, every screen reader user, every person who can't use a pointer. Use semantic HTML. Label every interactive element. Manage focus when modals open. Mark errors with role=alert. These are not extras. They are requirements.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the three production patterns from this lesson — Error Boundaries, Suspense with lazy loading, and accessibility — to a colleague preparing for a senior React interview. For each: what problem does it solve, how do you implement it, and what breaks if you skip it?

questions.prompt: Why must Error Boundaries be class components rather than function components?
options: They require the getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch lifecycle methods, which have no hook equivalents in React
Function components cannot render children
Error boundaries need access to the class's `this` keyword
React.lazy only works with class components
questions.answer: They require the getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch lifecycle methods, which have no hook equivalents in React
questions.explanation: getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch are class lifecycle methods for catching render-phase errors. As of React 18, there are no hook equivalents (though this may change in future versions). In practice, you write one ErrorBoundary class component and use it everywhere — you don't need to rewrite it. Libraries like react-error-boundary provide a hook-friendly wrapper.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of `React.lazy` combined with `Suspense`?
options: Code splitting — the component's JavaScript bundle is loaded on demand rather than in the initial bundle, reducing time-to-interactive
Lazy evaluation — the component only renders when it first enters the viewport
Suspense pauses the entire app while a component's props are being validated
React.lazy makes a component skip re-renders until its data is ready
questions.answer: Code splitting — the component's JavaScript bundle is loaded on demand rather than in the initial bundle, reducing time-to-interactive
questions.explanation: React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyPage')) tells the bundler to put HeavyPage in a separate chunk. When the component is first rendered, React downloads that chunk asynchronously. Suspense shows the fallback while the download is in progress. Large pages or rarely-visited routes loaded lazily can significantly reduce the initial bundle size and improve time-to-interactive.

questions.prompt: A modal opens but focus remains on the button that triggered it. A keyboard user cannot interact with the modal's content. What is the fix?
options: Use useRef on the first focusable element inside the modal and call ref.current.focus() in a useEffect that runs when open becomes true
Add tabIndex={0} to the modal's container div
Use autoFocus on the modal's container div
Set document.activeElement to the modal manually
questions.answer: Use useRef on the first focusable element inside the modal and call ref.current.focus() in a useEffect that runs when open becomes true
questions.explanation: When a modal opens, focus must move to the first focusable element inside it — typically the close button or the first form field. useEffect with the open dependency runs when open changes to true, and ref.current.focus() moves keyboard focus into the modal. Without this, keyboard and screen reader users are stuck — they can't access the modal content and can't interact with the page behind it either.

questions.prompt: A design spec calls for a clickable card that navigates to a detail page. A developer implements it as `<div onClick={navigate('/detail')}>`. What accessibility problems does this create?
options: Keyboard users can't activate it (not in tab order, no Enter/Space handler); screen readers don't announce it as interactive; the purpose is ambiguous to assistive technology
It works correctly — onClick handles all pointer and keyboard events automatically
Only the missing href is a problem — adding role='link' fixes everything
The div needs tabIndex={0} and that alone makes it accessible
questions.answer: Keyboard users can't activate it (not in tab order, no Enter/Space handler); screen readers don't announce it as interactive; the purpose is ambiguous to assistive technology
questions.explanation: A plain div is not focusable by default, not in the tab order, doesn't fire on Enter/Space, and is announced by screen readers as a generic container. Fixes: (1) Use a real <a href> or <button> — the browser handles all keyboard and accessibility behaviour for free. (2) If you must use a div: add tabIndex={0}, role='button' or role='link', and onKeyDown handlers for Enter/Space. Option 1 is always simpler and more correct.
